title: General Practical Physics II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L Practical Physics II curriculum: the second-semester practical companion to PHY107, covering electricity experiments (Ohm's law, series/parallel resistors, EMF and internal resistance, potentiometer, meter bridge), optics experiments (lens and mirror focal length, refractive index, prism spectrometer), waves experiments (resonance tube, sonometer), and basic magnetism/galvanometer lab skills.

questions.question: In an experiment to verify Ohm's law, a student plots a graph of potential difference (V) against current (I) for a metallic conductor at constant temperature. The expected shape of the graph is:
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a positive y-intercept
A curve that bends upward
A curve that bends downward
questions.correct_answer: A straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: Ohm's law states V = IR, so for a conductor held at constant temperature, V is directly proportional to I, giving a straight line through the origin whose gradient equals the resistance.

questions.question: In the Ohm's law experiment, the resistance of the conductor under test is obtained from the V-I graph as:
options: The gradient (slope) of the straight line
The y-intercept of the line
The x-intercept of the line
The area under the line
questions.correct_answer: The gradient (slope) of the straight line
questions.explanation: Since V = IR, R is the gradient of the V against I graph (change in V divided by change in I).

questions.question: In a circuit to verify Ohm's law, the ammeter must be connected:
options: In series with the conductor under test
In parallel with the conductor under test
In parallel with the battery only
In series with the voltmeter
questions.correct_answer: In series with the conductor under test
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures current, so it must be connected in series so that the full current through the conductor flows through it.

questions.question: In a circuit to verify Ohm's law, the voltmeter must be connected:
options: In parallel with the conductor under test
In series with the conductor under test
In series with the ammeter
Directly across the battery terminals only, never across the resistor
questions.correct_answer: In parallel with the conductor under test
questions.explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference across a component, so it must be connected in parallel (across) that component.

questions.question: An ideal ammeter should have:
options: Very low (ideally zero) resistance
Very high (ideally infinite) resistance
Resistance equal to the circuit's total resistance
Resistance that increases with current
questions.correct_answer: Very low (ideally zero) resistance
questions.explanation: An ammeter is connected in series, so it must have negligible resistance to avoid altering the current it is meant to measure.

questions.question: An ideal voltmeter should have:
options: Very high (ideally infinite) resistance
Very low (ideally zero) resistance
Resistance equal to the resistor it measures
Zero resistance when reversed
questions.correct_answer: Very high (ideally infinite) resistance
questions.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel, so it must draw negligible current from the branch to avoid disturbing the measured potential difference.

questions.question: Before starting a reading with an analogue ammeter or voltmeter of unknown magnitude, a student should:
options: Start on the highest current/voltage range and switch down as needed
Start on the lowest range to get maximum deflection immediately
Short-circuit the meter first to test it
Remove the meter's internal fuse
questions.correct_answer: Start on the highest current/voltage range and switch down as needed
questions.explanation: Starting on the highest range protects the meter from damage due to an unexpectedly large current or voltage; the range is then reduced to get a readable deflection.

questions.question: Two resistors of resistance 4 ohm and 6 ohm are connected in series. Their effective (equivalent) resistance is:
options: 10 ohm
2.4 ohm
24 ohm
5 ohm
questions.correct_answer: 10 ohm
questions.explanation: In series, resistances simply add: R = R1 + R2 = 4 + 6 = 10 ohm.

questions.question: Two resistors of resistance 4 ohm and 6 ohm are connected in parallel. Their effective (equivalent) resistance is closest to:
options: 2.4 ohm
10 ohm
24 ohm
1.5 ohm
questions.correct_answer: 2.4 ohm
questions.explanation: For parallel resistors, 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 12/5 = 2.4 ohm.

questions.question: In the series-resistors experiment, the equivalent resistance is verified by measuring the total voltage across the combination and:
options: The single current flowing through the whole series chain
The sum of the individual voltmeter readings only
The current at each resistor separately, since they differ
The resistance of the ammeter
questions.correct_answer: The single current flowing through the whole series chain
questions.explanation: In a series circuit the current is the same at every point, so R(total) = V(total)/I is obtained using the one common current value.

questions.question: In the parallel-resistors experiment, which quantity is the same across each branch of the combination?
options: The potential difference (voltage)
The current
The resistance
The power dissipated
questions.correct_answer: The potential difference (voltage)
questions.explanation: Resistors in parallel share the same two nodes, so the voltage across each branch is identical, while the current divides between branches according to each branch's resistance.

questions.question: In the experiment to determine the EMF and internal resistance of a cell, a graph of terminal potential difference (V) against current (I) is plotted. The EMF is obtained from this graph as:
options: The y-intercept (V when I = 0)
The gradient of the line
The x-intercept (I when V = 0)
The area under the graph
questions.correct_answer: The y-intercept (V when I = 0)
questions.explanation: From V = E - Ir, when I = 0 (no current drawn), V equals the EMF E, so the y-intercept of the V-I graph gives the EMF.

questions.question: In the experiment to determine the EMF and internal resistance of a cell, the internal resistance is obtained from the V-I graph as:
options: The magnitude of the gradient of the line
The y-intercept of the line
The reciprocal of the y-intercept
The product of V and I at any point
questions.correct_answer: The magnitude of the gradient of the line
questions.explanation: Since V = E - Ir, the equation has the form of a straight line with gradient -r; the internal resistance r is the magnitude of that negative gradient.

questions.question: In the EMF and internal resistance experiment, as more current is drawn from the cell by reducing an external variable resistor, the terminal potential difference:
options: Decreases, because more voltage is dropped across the internal resistance
Increases, because the cell works harder
Remains exactly constant and equal to the EMF
Becomes negative
questions.correct_answer: Decreases, because more voltage is dropped across the internal resistance
questions.explanation: As current increases, the voltage drop Ir across the cell's internal resistance increases, so the terminal voltage V = E - Ir falls below the EMF.

questions.question: A potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter for accurately measuring the EMF of a cell because, at balance:
options: No current is drawn from the cell being measured
It has a lower resistance than a voltmeter
It can measure current directly
It requires no calibration
questions.correct_answer: No current is drawn from the cell being measured
questions.explanation: At the balance (null) point, no current flows through the galvanometer branch and hence none is drawn from the cell under test, so its EMF is measured without a voltage drop due to internal resistance.

questions.question: In a potentiometer experiment comparing the EMFs of two cells, the ratio of the EMFs equals the ratio of:
options: Their respective balance lengths on the potentiometer wire
Their internal resistances
The currents drawn from each cell
The diameters of the potentiometer wire at balance
questions.correct_answer: Their respective balance lengths on the potentiometer wire
questions.explanation: Since the potential drop per unit length of the wire is uniform and constant, EMF is proportional to balance length, so E1/E2 = l1/l2.

questions.question: The galvanometer in a potentiometer or Wheatstone bridge circuit is used primarily to:
options: Detect the null (zero-current) point
Measure the exact value of current flowing
Supply current to the circuit
Measure resistance directly in ohms
questions.correct_answer: Detect the null (zero-current) point
questions.explanation: A galvanometer is a sensitive current detector; in bridge and potentiometer circuits it is used to detect when the current through it is zero (balance), not to read an exact current value.

questions.question: In a metre bridge (Wheatstone bridge form) experiment to find an unknown resistance, the bridge is said to be balanced when:
options: The galvanometer shows zero deflection
The galvanometer shows maximum deflection
The jockey is at the 100 cm end
The current through the unknown resistance is zero
questions.correct_answer: The galvanometer shows zero deflection
questions.explanation: Balance in a Wheatstone/metre bridge occurs when no current flows through the galvanometer branch, which is observed as zero deflection.

questions.question: In a metre bridge experiment, if the balance point is at a distance l cm from the end where the known resistance R is connected, and the bridge wire has total length 100 cm, the unknown resistance X is given by:
questions.explanation: At balance, R/X equals the ratio of the wire lengths on each side, l/(100-l) on the R side and the remainder on the X side; rearranging the standard metre-bridge balance condition R/l = X/(100-l) gives X = R(100-l)/l.

questions.question: To improve the accuracy of a metre bridge experiment, the balance point (jockey position) should ideally be located:
options: Near the middle of the wire (around 40-60 cm)
As close to the 0 cm end as possible
As close to the 100 cm end as possible
It does not matter where the balance point falls
questions.correct_answer: Near the middle of the wire (around 40-60 cm)
questions.explanation: Percentage error in reading the balance length is minimized when the balance point falls near the middle of the wire, so the known resistance box is adjusted until this occurs.

questions.question: To find the focal length of a converging (convex) lens by the no-parallax (plane mirror) method, the object pin and its image are coincident and free of parallax when:
options: The image pin does not appear to move relative to the object pin as the observer's eye is moved sideways
The image pin is exactly twice as tall as the object pin
The two pins touch each other physically
The lens is removed from the setup
questions.correct_answer: The image pin does not appear to move relative to the object pin as the observer's eye is moved sideways
questions.explanation: Parallax is the apparent relative displacement of two objects at different distances when the observer's viewpoint shifts; no-parallax means the image and search pin lie at exactly the same distance from the eye.

questions.question: In the plane-mirror (no-parallax) method for a convex lens, a plane mirror is placed behind the lens because at the position where the object coincides with its own image, the light must be:
options: Reflected straight back along its original path, meaning it struck the mirror normally after leaving the lens as a parallel beam
Refracted twice by the lens only
Diverging strongly from the mirror
Totally internally reflected inside the lens
questions.correct_answer: Reflected straight back along its original path, meaning it struck the mirror normally after leaving the lens as a parallel beam
questions.explanation: When the object pin is at the focal point of the lens, rays emerge parallel, strike the plane mirror normally, and retrace their path, forming a coincident image at the object pin itself -- so the object distance at coincidence equals the focal length.

questions.question: In the lens formula method for determining the focal length of a converging lens, a graph is often plotted of 1/v against 1/u. This graph is expected to be:
options: A straight line with intercepts of magnitude 1/f on both axes
A straight line passing through the origin
A parabola opening upward
A hyperbola with no intercepts
questions.correct_answer: A straight line with intercepts of magnitude 1/f on both axes
questions.explanation: The lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f (real-is-positive convention) rearranges to 1/v = 1/u + 1/f-type linear relation, so a graph of 1/v against 1/u is a straight line whose intercepts give 1/f.

questions.question: For a diverging (concave) lens, which method is typically used to determine its focal length experimentally, since it cannot form a real image of a real object alone?
options: Combining it with a converging lens (or using a real image as a virtual object) so a real final image is formed
Placing it directly in sunlight to burn a mark on paper
Using the no-parallax method exactly as for a convex lens with no modification
Measuring only its physical thickness with a micrometer
questions.correct_answer: Combining it with a converging lens (or using a real image as a virtual object) so a real final image is formed
questions.explanation: A diverging lens alone only forms virtual images of real objects, so it is combined with a converging lens (or a convergent beam is used) to create a real object/image situation from which the lens formula can be applied.

questions.question: To determine the focal length of a concave mirror using the no-parallax method, the object pin is adjusted until its position coincides with its own inverted image. At this position, the object distance from the mirror equals:
options: The radius of curvature of the mirror
The focal length of the mirror
Twice the focal length plus the radius
Half the focal length
questions.correct_answer: The radius of curvature of the mirror
questions.explanation: A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image coincident with the object only when the object is placed at the centre of curvature, where the object distance equals the radius of curvature R = 2f.

questions.question: In the mirror formula experiment (1/v + 1/u = 1/f) for a concave mirror, a graph of 1/v against 1/u gives a straight line. The focal length is obtained from this graph as:
options: The reciprocal of either intercept on the axes
The gradient of the line
The reciprocal of the gradient
The area enclosed by the line and the axes
questions.correct_answer: The reciprocal of either intercept on the axes
questions.explanation: The line has gradient -1 and intercepts of magnitude 1/f on both the 1/u and 1/v axes, so f is obtained by taking the reciprocal of an intercept.

questions.question: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, diminished, upright image of a real object, so its focal length is typically determined by:
options: Using it in combination with a converging lens or mirror to produce a real final image
Direct no-parallax coincidence with a real object
Placing the object exactly at the pole of the mirror
Measuring the mirror's physical curvature only with a ruler
questions.correct_answer: Using it in combination with a converging lens or mirror to produce a real final image
questions.explanation: Because a convex mirror alone cannot form a real image of a real object, an auxiliary converging lens or mirror is used to first form a real image that then acts as a virtual object for the convex mirror, allowing the mirror formula to be applied.

questions.question: In the real-depth/apparent-depth experiment to find the refractive index of a glass block using a travelling microscope or pins, the refractive index is calculated as:
options: Real depth divided by apparent depth
Apparent depth divided by real depth
Real depth minus apparent depth
The sum of real and apparent depth
questions.correct_answer: Real depth divided by apparent depth
questions.explanation: For near-normal viewing, the refractive index of the medium is given by n = real depth / apparent depth, since the glass block makes the mark appear closer to the surface than it really is.

questions.question: In the real/apparent depth experiment, the apparent depth is measured by locating the position where a travelling microscope, focused through the glass block, shows no parallax between the observed image and:
options: A search pin viewed above the glass block
The top surface of the glass block itself
A mark on the base of the microscope stand
The edge of the glass block
questions.correct_answer: A search pin viewed above the glass block
questions.explanation: A search pin is raised or lowered above the glass block until it shows no parallax with the image of the mark seen through the block, locating the apparent position of the mark.

questions.question: A student uses a glass block of real thickness 6.0 cm and measures an apparent thickness of 4.0 cm when viewed from directly above. The refractive index of the glass is:
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = real depth / apparent depth = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5, a typical value for glass.

questions.question: In the glass-block experiment for finding refractive index by tracing a ray with pins (incident and emergent ray method), the refractive index is calculated using:
options: Snell's law, from the measured angle of incidence and angle of refraction
The block's physical mass and volume
The distance between the two surfaces of the block only
The colour of the light source used
questions.correct_answer: Snell's law, from the measured angle of incidence and angle of refraction
questions.explanation: By tracing the incident and emergent rays with pins and measuring the angle of incidence and angle of refraction at the first surface, n = sin(i)/sin(r) is calculated directly from Snell's law.

questions.question: In the glass-block ray-tracing experiment, the lateral displacement of the emergent ray relative to the incident ray occurs because:
options: The ray refracts on entering and leaving the block along parallel surfaces, shifting its path sideways
Light travels faster inside glass than in air
The block absorbs part of the light beam
The emergent ray reflects internally before leaving
questions.correct_answer: The ray refracts on entering and leaving the block along parallel surfaces, shifting its path sideways
questions.explanation: Because the two faces of the block are parallel, the emergent ray leaves parallel to the incident ray but is laterally displaced due to the bending at each refracting surface.

questions.question: In the prism spectrometer experiment to determine the angle of minimum deviation, the deviation of a ray passing through a prism is at its minimum when:
options: The ray passes symmetrically through the prism, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of emergence
The prism is rotated to its maximum possible angle
The angle of incidence is exactly 90 degrees (grazing incidence)
The ray does not enter the prism at all
questions.correct_answer: The ray passes symmetrically through the prism, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of emergence
questions.explanation: Minimum deviation occurs at the symmetric ray path through the prism, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base.

questions.question: Using a spectrometer, the refractive index of a prism material is calculated from the measured angle of the prism (A) and the angle of minimum deviation (D_min) using the formula:
options: n = sin[(A + D_min)/2] / sin(A/2)
n = sin(A) / sin(D_min)
n = sin(D_min) / sin(A)
n = sin[(A - D_min)/2] / sin(A/2)
questions.correct_answer: n = sin[(A + D_min)/2] / sin(A/2)
questions.explanation: This is the standard prism formula relating refractive index to the prism angle A and the angle of minimum deviation D_min, derived from Snell's law applied at both faces under the symmetric minimum-deviation condition.

questions.question: Before taking readings with a prism spectrometer, the telescope and collimator must first be adjusted to be:
options: Focused for parallel rays (adjusted for infinity)
Focused for the nearest possible object
Tilted at 45 degrees to the bench
Pointed directly at the light source with the prism removed and left uncollimated
questions.correct_answer: Focused for parallel rays (adjusted for infinity)
questions.explanation: The collimator must produce a parallel beam and the telescope must be focused for parallel rays (set to infinity) so that accurate angle measurements can be made with the prism in the light path.

questions.question: In the prism angle (A) determination using a spectrometer, the prism angle is found by measuring the angle between two reflected images of the collimator slit from the two polished faces of the prism, and:
options: Halving the angle turned through by the telescope between the two reflected images
Doubling the angle turned through by the telescope
Reading it directly off the prism's engraved label
Measuring the base length of the prism with a ruler
questions.correct_answer: Halving the angle turned through by the telescope between the two reflected images
questions.explanation: The angle the telescope turns through between the two reflections is twice the prism angle A (by the geometry of reflection at each face), so A is obtained by halving the measured angle.

questions.question: In the resonance tube experiment to determine the velocity of sound in air, the air column is gradually lengthened by lowering the water level until the first position of resonance (loudest sound) is heard. This first resonance corresponds to an air column length of approximately:
options: A quarter of the wavelength of the sound (plus a small end correction)
Half the wavelength of the sound
The full wavelength of the sound
Twice the wavelength of the sound
questions.correct_answer: A quarter of the wavelength of the sound (plus a small end correction)
questions.explanation: A resonance tube closed at the water end and open at the top behaves as a closed pipe; its first resonance occurs when the air column length is one quarter of the wavelength, with a small end correction added for the antinode position just above the open end.

questions.question: In the resonance tube experiment, the difference in air column length between the first and second resonance positions for the same tuning fork corresponds to:
options: Half the wavelength of the sound
The full wavelength of the sound
A quarter of the wavelength of the sound
Twice the wavelength of the sound
questions.correct_answer: Half the wavelength of the sound
questions.explanation: Successive resonance positions in a closed pipe occur half a wavelength apart, so measuring the two resonance lengths and taking the difference doubles to give the wavelength, cancelling out the end correction.

questions.question: Using the resonance tube method, a student finds the first and second resonance lengths to be 18.0 cm and 56.0 cm for a tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz. The wavelength of the sound is:
questions.explanation: The distance between successive resonances equals half a wavelength: 56.0 - 18.0 = 38.0 cm = lambda/2, so lambda = 76.0 cm.

questions.question: Using the wavelength found from resonance-tube data (76.0 cm) with a tuning fork frequency of 512 Hz, the speed of sound in air is calculated as approximately:
options: 76 m/s
questions.explanation: Speed v = f x lambda = 512 Hz x 0.76 m = 389.1 m/s.

questions.question: The main source of systematic error to correct for in the simple resonance tube experiment (single closed-tube method, using only the first resonance) is:
options: The end correction, since the antinode forms slightly above the tube's open end
The speed of the water draining from the tube
The colour of the tube material
Air resistance acting on the water surface
questions.correct_answer: The end correction, since the antinode forms slightly above the tube's open end
questions.explanation: The pressure antinode does not form exactly at the open end of the tube but a small distance above it, so the effective length exceeds the measured air column length by this end correction, which the two-resonance method automatically cancels.

questions.question: In the sonometer experiment investigating the relationship between the frequency of a vibrating string and its length (at constant tension), the wire is adjusted until it resonates with a tuning fork, which is detected by:
options: A small paper rider placed on the wire being thrown off at resonance
The wire changing colour
The bridge under the wire melting
The wire becoming permanently magnetized
questions.correct_answer: A small paper rider placed on the wire being thrown off at resonance
questions.explanation: A light paper rider is placed on the sonometer wire; when the wire's vibration frequency matches the tuning fork's frequency, the wire vibrates with maximum amplitude at that point and throws the rider off, indicating resonance.

questions.question: In the sonometer experiment, at constant tension, the frequency of vibration of a stretched wire is found to be:
options: Inversely proportional to its vibrating length
Directly proportional to its vibrating length
Independent of its vibrating length
Proportional to the square of its vibrating length
questions.correct_answer: Inversely proportional to its vibrating length
questions.explanation: For a stretched string, f = (1/2L) x sqrt(T/mu); at constant tension T and linear density mu, frequency f is inversely proportional to the vibrating length L.

questions.question: In the sonometer experiment investigating frequency against tension (at constant length), a graph of frequency (f) against the square root of tension (sqrt(T)) is expected to be:
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a non-zero intercept
A parabola
A horizontal straight line
questions.correct_answer: A straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: Since f = (1/2L) x sqrt(T/mu), at constant L and mu, f is directly proportional to sqrt(T), giving a straight line through the origin when f is plotted against sqrt(T).

questions.question: On a sonometer, tension in the wire is typically applied and measured using:
options: Slotted masses hung over a pulley at one end of the wire
A spring embedded inside the wire itself
The weight of the bridges only
An electric motor that twists the wire
questions.correct_answer: Slotted masses hung over a pulley at one end of the wire
questions.explanation: In the standard sonometer setup, one end of the wire passes over a pulley and known slotted masses are hung from it, so the tension equals the weight of the masses (mg).

questions.question: When plotting magnetic field lines around a bar magnet using a plotting compass and iron filings, the field lines are drawn such that they:
options: Emerge from the north pole and re-enter at the south pole outside the magnet
Emerge from the south pole and re-enter at the north pole
Form closed loops that never touch the magnet
Are always straight and parallel regardless of magnet shape
questions.correct_answer: Emerge from the north pole and re-enter at the south pole outside the magnet
questions.explanation: By convention, magnetic field lines outside a magnet run from the north pole to the south pole, and continue through the interior of the magnet from south back to north, forming closed loops.

questions.question: In the plotting-compass method for tracing magnetic field lines, the neutral point (where the magnet's field exactly cancels the Earth's horizontal magnetic field) is identified as the point where:
options: The compass needle shows no preferred direction and can point any way
The compass needle points due north regardless of position
The compass needle spins continuously
Iron filings refuse to align at all points on the paper
questions.correct_answer: The compass needle shows no preferred direction and can point any way
questions.explanation: At a neutral point, the magnet's field and the Earth's horizontal field are equal and opposite, cancelling to zero net field, so the compass needle has no restoring torque and can rest in any orientation.

questions.question: A moving-coil galvanometer is converted into an ammeter of a required range by connecting:
options: A low-resistance shunt in parallel with the galvanometer
A high-resistance multiplier in series with the galvanometer
A capacitor in series with the galvanometer
Nothing; the galvanometer is used directly
questions.correct_answer: A low-resistance shunt in parallel with the galvanometer
questions.explanation: A shunt resistor of low resistance is connected in parallel with the galvanometer coil so that most of the current bypasses the coil, extending its range to read larger currents as an ammeter.

questions.question: A moving-coil galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter of a required range by connecting:
options: A high-resistance multiplier (resistor) in series with the galvanometer
A low-resistance shunt in parallel with the galvanometer
An inductor in parallel with the galvanometer
The galvanometer directly across the supply with no extra component
questions.correct_answer: A high-resistance multiplier (resistor) in series with the galvanometer
questions.explanation: A high-value resistor (multiplier) is connected in series with the galvanometer so that only a small, proportional fraction of the total voltage appears across the sensitive coil, allowing it to read larger voltages as a voltmeter.

questions.question: In an experiment involving a delicate galvanometer, before switching on the circuit for the first time a student should include a high protective resistance in the circuit mainly to:
options: Limit the initial current and prevent damage to the galvanometer coil
Increase the sensitivity of the reading
Reduce the EMF of the battery
Make the pointer move faster
questions.correct_answer: Limit the initial current and prevent damage to the galvanometer coil
questions.explanation: A protective (safety) resistance limits the current when the circuit is first closed or when far from balance, preventing an excessive current from damaging the sensitive galvanometer coil.

questions.question: When recording data in any of these practical experiments (electricity, optics, waves), the recommended practice for uncertainty in a repeated measurement is to:
options: Take several readings, average them, and estimate the uncertainty from the spread of the readings
Take only one reading and assume it is exact
Discard all readings except the first one taken
Record only the final calculated result, without the raw readings
questions.correct_answer: Take several readings, average them, and estimate the uncertainty from the spread of the readings
questions.explanation: Good experimental practice requires repeated readings to reduce the effect of random error, with the average taken as the best estimate and the spread used to estimate the associated uncertainty.

questions.question: If the fractional (percentage) errors in two independently measured quantities x and y are combined to find the fractional error in a derived quantity Q = xy, the correct approach is to:
options: Add the fractional errors in x and y
Multiply the fractional errors in x and y
Subtract the fractional errors in x and y
Take the average of the absolute errors in x and y
questions.correct_answer: Add the fractional errors in x and y
questions.explanation: For a quantity formed by multiplying (or dividing) measured quantities, the fractional (relative) errors are added in quadrature or simply added as an upper-bound estimate; multiplying or subtracting them is not correct error propagation.

questions.question: A student obtains a very scattered set of points when plotting a V-I graph for the Ohm's law experiment, with no clear straight-line trend. The most likely cause is:
options: Poor contact in the circuit or a faulty/loose connection causing unstable readings
The conductor obeying Ohm's law too precisely
The ammeter and voltmeter being too accurate
Using graph paper instead of plain paper
questions.correct_answer: Poor contact in the circuit or a faulty/loose connection causing unstable readings
questions.explanation: Scattered, inconsistent readings in a circuit experiment most commonly result from loose or dirty connections causing intermittent contact resistance, rather than a genuine departure from Ohm's law.

questions.question: In the no-parallax method for lenses and mirrors, a common source of error is:
options: Parallax not being fully eliminated, so the search pin position is misjudged
The pin being made of metal
The bench being too long
Using a lens holder instead of holding the lens by hand
questions.correct_answer: Parallax not being fully eliminated, so the search pin position is misjudged
questions.explanation: If the observer does not carefully check for relative movement between the image and the search pin from several viewing angles, residual parallax leads to an incorrect location of the image, introducing error into u, v, or f.

questions.question: In the metre bridge experiment, a systematic error known as 'end error' or 'end resistance' arises mainly from:
options: Contact resistance at the copper strip junctions near the ends of the bridge wire
The colour of the bridge wire
The length of the connecting leads to the battery
The type of galvanometer used
questions.correct_answer: Contact resistance at the copper strip junctions near the ends of the bridge wire
questions.explanation: Small, often unequal contact resistances at the metal strip-to-wire junctions near the two ends of the bridge wire introduce a systematic 'end error', which can be corrected for by interchanging the resistances and averaging.

questions.question: In the resonance tube and sonometer experiments, a key source of error affecting frequency-related results is:
options: Using a tuning fork whose frequency is not accurately known, or one that has decayed in amplitude
The colour of the tuning fork
Using a wooden retort stand instead of a metal one
Measuring length with a ruler instead of a stopwatch
questions.correct_answer: Using a tuning fork whose frequency is not accurately known, or one that has decayed in amplitude
questions.explanation: The accuracy of derived quantities like the speed of sound or wire tension relies directly on the stated frequency of the tuning fork being correct and the fork being struck to give a clear, sustained tone.

questions.question: In the prism spectrometer experiment, parallax error between the cross-wires of the telescope and the image of the slit is minimized by:
options: Adjusting the eyepiece so the cross-wires are sharply focused and coincide with the image with no relative shift on eye movement
Using a brighter light source only
Increasing the prism angle
Reducing the collimator slit width to zero
questions.correct_answer: Adjusting the eyepiece so the cross-wires are sharply focused and coincide with the image with no relative shift on eye movement
questions.explanation: As with other optical no-parallax checks, the eyepiece cross-wires must be focused so that they show no relative displacement with the slit image as the observer's eye moves, ensuring accurate angular readings.

questions.question: A student measures a resistor using a metre bridge and obtains 100 cm exactly as the balance length (i.e., the balance point falls right at the very end of the wire). This result should be treated with suspicion mainly because:
options: The known resistance in the resistance box is likely far too small or too large relative to the unknown, pushing the balance point to an extreme where percentage error is largest
It is a perfectly valid and highly accurate reading
The bridge wire is too short to be used at all
The galvanometer must be broken
questions.correct_answer: The known resistance in the resistance box is likely far too small or too large relative to the unknown, pushing the balance point to an extreme where percentage error is largest
questions.explanation: A balance point at or very near either end of the wire indicates a poor choice of comparison resistance, and readings near the ends carry the largest relative error in length measurement; the resistance box value should be adjusted to bring balance nearer the middle.

questions.question: Which of the following apparatus is essential for the experiment to determine the focal length of a converging lens by the no-parallax method?
options: An optical pin (object pin), a search pin, a plane mirror, and a metre rule
A prism, a spectrometer, and a sodium lamp
A sonometer wire and slotted masses
An ammeter, voltmeter, and rheostat
questions.correct_answer: An optical pin (object pin), a search pin, a plane mirror, and a metre rule
questions.explanation: The plane-mirror no-parallax method for a convex lens requires an object pin, a search pin to locate the image, a plane mirror placed behind the lens, and a metre rule to measure distances.

questions.question: In an experiment on resistors in parallel, three resistors of 2 ohm, 3 ohm, and 6 ohm are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
options: 1 ohm
11 ohm
0.33 ohm
3 ohm
questions.correct_answer: 1 ohm

questions.question: In the potentiometer experiment for measuring internal resistance of a cell, a balance length l1 is obtained with the cell on open circuit, and a shorter balance length l2 is obtained when a known resistance R is connected across the cell as an external load. The internal resistance r is given by:
options: r = Rl2/l1
questions.explanation: Since balance length is proportional to potential difference, l1 corresponds to the EMF and l2 to the terminal p.d. across R; using E = I(R + r) and V = IR with lengths substituted for potentials gives r = R(l1 - l2)/l2.

questions.question: In the sonometer experiment, the linear density (mass per unit length) of the wire, mu, affects the resonant frequency such that, at constant length and tension, frequency is:
options: Inversely proportional to the square root of mu
Directly proportional to mu
Independent of mu
Directly proportional to the square root of mu
questions.correct_answer: Inversely proportional to the square root of mu
questions.explanation: From f = (1/2L) x sqrt(T/mu), at constant L and T, frequency decreases as mu increases, following an inverse square-root relationship -- this is why thicker (higher mass per length) strings give lower notes.
